title: Meeting at one place
summary: Rendezvous and gathering on graphs, gathering and convergence in the plane, and evacuation through an unknown exit all ask entities to end at one point. The papers give the same reasons for meeting, but each model makes a different part of it hard: symmetry and exploration on graphs, capability in the plane, information in continuous search.

sections.heading: Why the papers want entities to meet
sections.body:
The reasons given are practical and much the same in every model. Robots exploring a terrain meet "to exchange samples of the ground previously collected by the robots, or exchange information obtained when exploring different parts of the terrain", and software agents meet periodically "to exchange collected data and plan further actions" [Pelc2019Survey]. Bouchard, Dieudonné and Pelc add mobile robots "moving along corridors of a contaminated mine that is not accessible to humans", and give as reasons to gather samples or "to coordinate some future task, such as network maintenance or finding a map of the network" [Bouchard2023Chatter]. In the plane, gathering is called "one of the most fundamental tasks one can ask mobile robots to perform, e.g. to collect acquired data or to update the robots' algorithm" [Bramas2023Indulgent].

The second reason is that meeting is a building block. Gathering "turns out to be an essential prerequisite to achieve more complex cooperative works", so that results on gathering are results on everything built on it [Bouchard2022Polynomial]; Devismes, Dieudonné and Labourel use almost the same words [Devismes2026Homonymous]. Clement et al. place gathering among agreement problems: like scattering, it is "similar to the consensus problem in conventional distributed systems", with simple definitions but solvability that "greatly depends on the synchrony of the systems as well as the nature of the faults" [Clement2010Cost].

sections.heading: On graphs: first break symmetry, then explore
sections.body:
Pelc separates rendezvous settings by whether agents can see something other than the environment, other agents or marks [Pelc2019Survey]. On graphs they usually cannot, and two conventions fix the difficulty. Nodes are anonymous because "if nodes had distinct labels, then agents might explore the graph and meet in the smallest node, hence gathering would reduce to the well-studied task of exploration"; ports are numbered because without them "the adversary could prevent an agent from taking some edge" [Bouchard2023Chatter]. Identical agents may never meet: two of them starting together on a ring with consistent ports run forever in parallel [TaShma2014Deterministic]. So the labels of the agents are the symmetry breaker, and the cost is polynomial in $n$ and the label length [Dessmark2006Deterministic] [TaShma2014Deterministic]. In trees the cost is $\Theta(n+\log\lambda)$, where $\lambda$ is the smaller label [Dessmark2006Deterministic]. Ta-Shma and Zwick also posed treasure hunt, rendezvous in which one agent never moves, as a tool for this question [TaShma2014Deterministic].

Without labels the question becomes which initial configurations can meet. Dieudonné and Pelc characterise the configurations of identical agents that can gather, and show that detecting that gathering is complete needs a bound on $n$ [Dieudonne2016Anonymous]. For two identical asynchronous agents, meeting is feasible exactly when their views differ or their starting nodes are joined by a path whose port sequence is a palindrome [Guilbault2011Asynchronous], as summarised in [Pelc2019Survey]. A middle ground is homonymous agents, motivated by cost and privacy: unique labels "can be costly", and agents "may deliberately blur their identity by revealing it only partially" [Devismes2026Homonymous]. With asynchronous agents the adversary controls speeds and agents may meet inside an edge; polynomial cost was reached only in [Dieudonne2015Polynomial], after the ring case [DeMarco2006Asynchronous].

sections.heading: In the plane: first ask whether it is possible
sections.body:
Robots in the plane see each other, so finding the others is not the issue; agreeing on a point is. Prencipe states the research question as "under which conditions this task can be accomplished by the robots?", and shows that without extra assumptions such as multiplicity detection gathering is in general impossible [Prencipe2007Impossibility]. Suzuki and Yamashita had shown that two oblivious robots cannot meet in SSYNC [Suzuki1999Formation], and Flocchini et al. explain why two robots matter: rendezvous "separates FSynch from SSynch for oblivious robots", whereas $n \ge 3$ robots gather even in ASYNC with multiplicity detection [Flocchini2016Constant] [Cieliebak2012Gathering]. Izumi et al. note that, for semi-synchronous robots, two-robot gathering is the single pattern that memory makes formable [Izumi2012TwoRobots].

That made rendezvous the test case for every new capability. Unreliable compasses solve it below a threshold deviation [Izumi2012TwoRobots]. A light with two colours solves it in ASYNC [Das2016Lights] [Heriban2018Optimally], and three colours suffice when a robot sees only its own light (FSTA, in SSYNC) or only the other's (FCOM, even in ASYNC) [Flocchini2016Constant], and three colours are also necessary [Otaka2026TwoState]. The measure throughout is feasibility and the number of colours, not time.

sections.heading: Convergence: giving up the exact point
sections.body:
Relaxing the goal removes most of the difficulty. Izumi et al. remark in passing that "Two oblivious robots can converge to a point with a naive algorithm that consists of always moving toward the midpoint of their positions" [Izumi2012TwoRobots]. Convergence of $n$ robots was given by Suzuki and Yamashita [Suzuki1999Formation], with limited visibility by Ando et al. the same year [Ando1999Convergence], and the centre of gravity converges in ASYNC [Cohen2005Gravitational].

With convergence and with limited visibility, time becomes measurable again, and the bounds are about locality. Under limited visibility in FSYNC, a class of local protocols needs and achieves $\Theta(\Delta_0^2)$ rounds, where $\Delta_0$ is the initial diameter in units of the visibility range [Castenow2022Unifying]; near-gathering, in which robots must come close without colliding [Pagli2015Near], takes $O(\Delta_0^2)$ epochs for disoriented robots in SSYNC, again tight within that class [Castenow2022Unifying]. With rigid moves and a common compass, asynchronous gathering takes $\Theta(\Delta_0)$ epochs; with one common axis the same time only brings the robots onto a horizontal segment of length 1 [Poudel2021TimeOptimal].

sections.heading: In continuous search: meeting at a point nobody chose
sections.body:
Evacuation fixes the meeting point in advance but hides it. Bampas et al. set the three measures side by side: in search the cost is the arrival of the first searcher at a target placed by an adversary; in rendezvous it is the arrival of the last robot, and "the meeting point is arbitrary, i.e., the robots may choose the most convenient one"; in their linear search problem "a pair of robots has to meet at an unknown fixed target point of the environment" and the cost is the arrival of the second [Bampas2019Speeds]. Evacuation is this third problem.

Czyzowicz et al., posing evacuation from a disk, describe the tension: robots should spread to find the exit fast but not so far that the walk to it becomes long [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]. Communication decides how much the meeting costs. Two wireless robots evacuate in exactly $1+2\pi/3+\sqrt3 \approx 4.826$ [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]; with face-to-face communication the best algorithm takes about $5.6234$ [Disser2019Second] against a lower bound of about $5.255$ [Czyzowicz2020FaceToFace]. On the line, face-to-face robots that must all reach the target cannot beat the single-robot ratio 9 [Bampas2019Speeds] [Chrobak2015GroupSearch].

sections.heading: One task, three difficulties
sections.body:
Read across the models, meeting is hard for three different reasons. On graphs agents cannot see each other, so meeting needs exploration and symmetry breaking, and the open questions are about cost: labelled rendezvous is polynomial, but the exponent is far from the lower bound (see the rendezvous page). In the plane robots see each other but cannot remember or agree, so the open questions are about which capabilities suffice and how many colours they need. In continuous search robots know the domain and each other's plans but not the target, so the open questions are gaps between constants.

Faults sharpen each version differently: $f$ Byzantine agents on graphs require $f+1$ good agents, or $f+2$ when the number $n$ of nodes is unknown [Bouchard2016Byzantine]; one Byzantine robot among three already prevents gathering in the plane in SSYNC [Agmon2006Fault]; and a faulty robot in a disk raises the evacuation time [Czyzowicz2017Faulty]. The perspective *When agents fail* follows that thread.
